title: Mezze spread
skill: A spread for guests, held safely

notes.text: Cook the chickpeas in two pots, and roast the eggplant on two pans so it chars instead of steaming.

move.title: A table of small plates
move.body: A Lebanese mezze is many small dishes shared at once. You'll cook hummus from dried chickpeas, roast eggplant for baba ghanoush, mince a tabbouleh, and dress labneh, then set it all out for guests. This is the unit's mastery week: two of the dips are cooked hot and served cold, so the skill is cooling them fast and holding the whole table below 41°F.

why.title: Soak, then soda
why.body: An overnight soak lets dried chickpeas absorb water evenly, so they cook in about an hour instead of three. A little baking soda in the cooking water raises the pH and breaks down the skins, which is what makes hummus from dried chickpeas smoother than from a can.

why.title: Cooling in two stages
why.body: Cooked food passes through the danger zone on its way down. The FDA's rule is from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F within 4 more. Spread shallow on a sheet pan, hot chickpeas and eggplant make the first stage easily; a deep pot of them would not.

why.title: Char the skin, steam the inside
why.body: Eggplant roasted whole at high heat chars on the outside while the flesh steams in its own skin until it collapses. The char gives baba ghanoush its smoky taste; the soft flesh mashes smooth.

why.title: Drain the eggplant
why.body: Roasted eggplant releases a lot of brown, bitter liquid. Ten minutes in a colander leaves a thicker, cleaner-tasting dip.

why.title: Ice water in hummus
why.body: A few tablespoons of ice water added while the blender runs whip air into the hummus and lighten its color. Warm liquid makes it dense.

why.title: Hold it like a buffet
why.body: Every dip here is a perishable food. Set out on ice in small bowls, probed every 30 minutes, and refilled from the fridge on clean bowls, it stays below 41°F. Off ice, it has 2 hours.

wrong.sign: The chickpeas are still firm after an hour
wrong.fix: Keep simmering, checking every 10 minutes. Old chickpeas take longer; one should crush to a paste between your fingers.
The chickpeas weren't soft enough. Simmer the rest longer next time, and blend at least 3 minutes.

wrong.sign: The baba ghanoush is bitter and watery
wrong.fix: It wasn't drained. Spoon it into a strainer for 10 minutes and stir in another spoon of tahini.

wrong.sign: The chickpeas are still warm after 2 hours
wrong.fix: They were too deep. Spread them thinner and put the pan in the fridge; next time cool them on a sheet pan from the start.

quiz.q: What does baking soda do in the chickpeas' cooking water?
choices: Breaks down the skins so the hummus is smoother

quiz.q: What is the two-stage cooling rule?
choices: 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours, then to 41°F in 4 more
Its liquid is bitter and thins the dip

quiz.q: How long can the dips sit out off ice?

ingredients.prep: for the tabbouleh, labneh, and tops of the dips

substitutions.note: Toast gluten-free bread in strips. Swap the tabbouleh's bulgur for cooked quinoa.

steps.text: The night before, weigh the chickpeas, pick out any stones, and cover them with 5 cm of cold water in the large bowl. Leave them to soak overnight.
Drain the chickpeas, cover them by 5 cm with fresh water in the pot, and add the baking soda. Bring to a boil, skim the foam, and simmer partly covered.
While they simmer, heat the oven to 475°F. Prick the eggplants all over with a fork and roast them on a foil-lined sheet pan, turning once, until collapsed.
Bring ⅓ cup of water to a boil in the saucepan, pour it over the bulgur in the small bowl, and cover.
Mince the parsley and mint fine, dice the tomatoes at 6 mm, and slice the green onions thin. Combine in the medium bowl.
steps.look: Herbs the size of a grain of rice, bright green, no paste.

steps.text: Check the chickpeas: one should crush to a paste between your fingers. Simmer longer if not. Drain, saving 1 cup of the liquid.
Spread the chickpeas on a sheet pan to cool. Probe them and write down the time; they must reach 70°F within 2 hours.
Take out the eggplant and turn off the oven. When you can handle it, split it, scoop the flesh into the colander, and let it drain.
Mince both garlic cloves to a paste with a pinch of the hummus's salt, and split it between two small piles.

Blend the chickpeas, hummus tahini, lemon juice, one pile of garlic, the rest of its salt, and the cumin. With the motor running, add ice water a tablespoon at a time, then up to ¼ cup of the cooking liquid, until smooth.
Chop the drained eggplant, then mash it with a fork with its tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and salt.
steps.look: Creamy with some texture, pale brown flecked with char.

steps.text: Fluff the bulgur, add it to the herbs with the tabbouleh's lemon juice and salt and ¼ cup of the oil, and toss.
Cover the hummus, baba ghanoush, and tabbouleh and refrigerate them in shallow containers until each probes 41°F or below.
steps.look: 41°F or below in the center of each.

steps.text: Spread the labneh in a shallow bowl, make a well with the back of a spoon, and fill it with oil. Dust with sumac.
Spoon each dip into a small bowl, swirl, and add a thread of oil. Set the bowls in a tray of ice. Warm the pita and cut it into wedges.
Probe a dip every 30 minutes and log it. Refill on clean bowls from the fridge. At 2 hours, or any reading above 41°F, take it all in: refrigerate what held 41°F on ice, and discard the rest.
